title: From Mumbai to Rishikesh: Retirees Choose Tier-2 Cities and Spiritual Hubs
excerpt: Senior living's growth frontier is shifting to Coimbatore, Mysuru, Haridwar and Ayodhya as India's elderly population heads toward 230 million by 2036.
body:
• India's senior-living market is projected to grow from $4.31 billion in 2026 to $11.43 billion by 2031, with Tier-2 cities and spiritual hubs the next growth centres, Square Yards Research finds.
  • The pull is arithmetic: lower land, construction and living costs in cities such as Coimbatore, Mysuru, Vadodara, Nashik and Kochi, while spiritual hubs Tirupati, Haridwar, Varanasi and Ayodhya — and Rishikesh in the wider trend — add community and faith.
  • India's 60-plus population is projected to rise from 143 million in 2021 to about 230 million by 2036; senior-living penetration is only about 1.5%, versus 6-7% in the US.
  • For NRI families weighing a return: judge a Tier-2 move on hospital access, emergency response and trained caregiving first — the report warns affordability alone does not make a project work.

Retirement in India is moving down the city rankings. A growing number of retirees are choosing Tier-2 cities and spiritual hubs over metros such as Mumbai, according to the trend examined by India Today, and the money is following them: India's senior-living market is projected to grow from $4.31 billion in 2026 to $11.43 billion by 2031, Square Yards Research estimates in its report "Expanding Horizons: The Next Growth Markets for Senior Living in India."

The numbers behind the move

The demographic pressure is large. India's population aged 60 and above is projected to increase from 143 million in 2021 to nearly 230 million by 2036, Outlook Money reported from the same study. Yet formal senior living remains thin: penetration is around 1.5% in India, compared with 6 to 7% in the United States and 14 to 15% in New Zealand, according to ET Edge Insights' summary of the report.

Developers are responding with capital. The report records DLF's entry into senior living in Gurugram, a planned Rs 3,000-crore investment by Columbia Pacific's Serene Communities across multiple cities, and a Rs 2,000-crore platform from Primus Senior Living and HDFC Capital.

Which cities, and why

Square Yards names Coimbatore, Tirupati, Haridwar, Varanasi and Ayodhya among the emerging destinations, and highlights Coimbatore, Mysuru, Vadodara, Nashik and Kochi for their combination of comparatively affordable property, available land, healthcare access and established community networks. Lower land and construction costs let developers build larger campuses with shared amenities — physiotherapy rooms, diagnostics, pharmacies, in-apartment emergency alerts, yoga and meditation spaces.

Spiritual destinations form a distinct category. Tirupati, Haridwar, Varanasi and Ayodhya appeal to retirees seeking proximity to religious sites, familiar cultural settings and wellness-oriented routines — the same logic that draws retirees toward Rishikesh. Tier-1 markets Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Chennai will keep attracting demand for their healthcare ecosystems, with Hyderabad showing the highest projected growth rate through 2031, but the growth frontier is smaller cities.

The caveats that decide whether it works

The report is clear that a cheap plot is not a retirement plan. A spiritual hub's long-term potential depends on hospital access, transport connectivity and professional care services; across the sector, affordability constraints, limited awareness and gaps in trained caregiving remain barriers, and many families still prefer family-based care.

For diaspora families planning a parent's move — or their own return — the checklist from the research is concrete: verify tertiary hospital access and emergency response in the specific city, confirm who operates the community day to day, and price the ongoing service and healthcare charges, not just the purchase. Where those align, the Tier-2 and spiritual-hub route now offers what the metros increasingly do not: space, community and a slower pace at a cost a pension can carry.
